newsitem.title: USA: Calif. Treasurer urges penalties for Texaco execs.
newsitem.headline: Calif. Treasurer urges penalties for Texaco execs.

text.p: California state Treasurer Matt Fong on Monday urged Texaco Inc's board of directors to withhold or cut annual bonuses given to company executives in response to the company's discrimination scandal.
"I formally request the board of directors of Texaco to cut or withhold bonuses to the senior officers of Texaco for this year," Fong said.
"Accountability should be borne by those who were in position to prevent what happened and are in the best position to prevent this from happening again," the treasurer said.
The California Public Employees' Retirement System (PERS) and the State Teachers' Retirement System (STRS) hold roughly two million shares of Texaco stock, Fong said.
Fong, who serves on the boards of the pension funds, said he was prepared to use the funds to influence Texaco.

"If Texaco's board of directors fail to hold senior officers accountable, then I will take this matter to the boards of PERS and STRS and request that they use their influence to seek support from other pension funds across the nation to force the directors to hold senior management accountable," Fong said at a press briefing in Sacramento.
Fong said any divestiture of Texaco stock would be "misdirected" because top executives would not be impacted and state pension funds could be hurt.

"I believe that boycotts and divestitures punish the wrong individuals," Fong said. "Attacking the bonuses of senior management, compensation used to reward extraordinary results, is not only fair game, but it is more focused."
The Philadelphia pension board voted last week to divest $5.5 million worth of Texaco stock, citing what it called evidence of racial bias at the oil company.
The divestiture came after reports that tape recordings of discussions among Texaco executives were laced with racial slurs.
The Texaco tapes came to light in connection with a racial discrimination lawsuit filed against Texaco by six black employees.
